summary: This informational memo lists what Nimrod, an experimental routing architecture, needs from any multicast solution. Nimrod does not pick one multicast technique itself, so the document states requirements and approaches.

eli5.summary: Before you pick a bus to take the whole class, you first write down what the bus must be able to do.

questions: how to send messages to multiple recipients
subtitle: What a routing architecture needs to support one-to-many message delivery.

tldr.problem: Applications like videoconferencing need to send one message to many recipients at once, but Nimrod, an experimental routing architecture, did not specify how to support this.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists the requirements that Nimrod places on any multicast solution and compares existing approaches including DVMRP, Core-Based Trees, Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM), MOSPF and IDPR.
tldr.outcome: Nimrod remains flexible by allowing multiple multicast approaches as long as they meet its requirements. The document shows how PIM in particular can be implemented within Nimrod.

today: RFC 2102 is informational and has not been obsoleted. While Nimrod itself was an experimental architecture that did not see wide deployment, the multicast design problems it identifies remain relevant, and PIM has become a widely deployed multicast protocol in modern Internet infrastructure.

sections.title: Multicast in Nimrod
sections.content:
Nimrod is an experimental architecture for routing and addressing in the Internet, designed to be flexible and adaptable. Unlike earlier routing systems, Nimrod does not specify a particular solution for multicasting—the problem of efficiently sending one message to multiple recipients. Instead, the architecture allows different implementations to use different multicast techniques, as long as they meet Nimrod's core requirements.

This approach stems from two practical reasons. First, multicasting is a complex problem whose requirements were still being understood at the time. Second, other IETF working groups were already studying multicast separately, and Nimrod preferred not to duplicate that effort. Instead, this document lists what Nimrod demands from any multicast solution and evaluates five existing approaches.
sections.eli5: Nimrod says 'we don't care how you send a message to many people, as long as you do it efficiently.' This document lists what we mean by efficient and shows which techniques could work.

sections.title: What Makes Multicast Different
sections.content:
Multicast differs from regular unicast (one sender, one receiver) routing in three important ways. First, multicast has dynamic group membership: recipients join and leave groups at runtime, so the system must adapt incrementally instead of rebuilding paths from scratch. Second, state creation can be initiated by the sender, the receivers, or the routers themselves—different approaches have different trade-offs. Third, route generation in multicast offers many heuristics: some produce low-cost trees with higher delay, others give shortest paths but with higher cost.

Because many combinations of these approaches exist and each suits different applications, Nimrod avoids mandating one solution. However, for routers to interoperate, they must agree on the structure of the forwarding state they create, even if different implementations build that state in different ways.
sections.eli5: Sending to many people is trickier than sending to one because people are always joining and leaving the group, and there's no single 'best' path—sometimes cheap is better, sometimes fast is better.

sections.title: Nimrod's Multicast Requirements
sections.content:
Nimrod identifies four core requirements for multicast support. Scalability is paramount: the system must scale to large networks, many groups and many members per group. Routers not on the path to destinations should not be involved, group membership changes must be handled incrementally, and the solution must work for both sparse (few members) and dense (many members) group distributions.

Policy support means every path from source to destination must satisfy quality-of-service bounds and access restrictions. The system must know where destinations are located and respect domain-specific policies. Resource sharing requires that the architecture interact well with resource reservation protocols, clearly marking which tree resources are shareable. Interoperability demands that the multicast solution work independently of any particular unicast routing protocol, and that different multicast implementations can coexist in the same network.
sections.eli5: For multicast to work well in Nimrod, it needs to handle huge numbers of people and groups without slowing down the network, respect rules about which traffic is allowed where, tell the network how to reserve resources fairly, and work even if different routers use different multicast methods.

sections.title: Five Multicast Approaches
sections.content:
The document evaluates five existing or proposed multicast techniques. DVMRP (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol) uses reverse-path forwarding to build sender-based shortest-path trees, but scales poorly with many sources and groups. Core-Based Trees uses a single shared tree per group rooted at a core router, reducing state overhead to just O(G) but risking suboptimal paths and traffic concentration. PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) bridges these by supporting both shared trees and source-based trees, working well for both sparse and dense groups but adding complexity.

MOSPF (Multicast Open Shortest Path First) computes shortest-path trees using link-state topology, guaranteeing optimality but broadcasting group membership throughout the network. IDPR (Inter-Domain Policy Routing) uses the source to compute policy-aware multicast routes and set up forwarding state, enabling strong policy support but making membership changes difficult.
sections.eli5: Different techniques trade off between simple-but-wasteful, cheap-but-slow, fast-but-complex, optimal, and policy-aware. Each works best for different situations.

sections.title: Implementing PIM in Nimrod
sections.content:
As a concrete example, the document shows how PIM-style multicast can be implemented using Nimrod's forwarding modes. In PIM, routers join multicast groups at a rendezvous point, and sources send traffic to that point. Receivers then either stay on the shared tree (for cost efficiency) or switch to source-based shortest-path trees (for lower delay).

Nimrod's path-setup facility and link-state topology maps make this straightforward. Designated routers can generate routes to the rendezvous point, join and leave trees as group membership changes, and switch between shared and source-rooted trees as needed. The flexibility of Nimrod's architecture means that PIM, IDPR-like approaches, or MOSPF-like schemes could all coexist in the same network, each implementation choosing the approach best suited to its needs.
sections.eli5: Nimrod has the right building blocks to support PIM and other multicast methods. Different routers can use different methods and still work together as long as they agree on how to store forwarding information.

references.text: Calvert, K., Bhattacharjee, S., Sterbenz, J., "Nimrod Routing Architecture", 1996.
